title: Feijoada
subtitle: Brazilian black bean and pork stew with rice and farofa
excerpt: Brazil's national dish: a rich, slow-cooked stew of black beans and pork, served with rice, fried kale and orange slices. This is a Saturday ritual across Brazil, made for large family gatherings. It takes time but rewards patience with deep, smoky flavour.
sourceNotes: Feijoada is Brazil's national dish, with roots in the traditions of enslaved Africans who combined pork offal and black beans on plantations. Today it is a Saturday ritual across Brazil, eaten in large family gatherings and served with rice, fried kale, orange slices and farofa.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the stew for up to 3 months. Cook rice fresh to serve.
recipe.batchNotes: Feijoada is traditionally made in very large quantities for a crowd.

glossaryTerms.definition: Toasted cassava flour, a staple condiment in Brazilian cooking. It is sprinkled over feijoada and other dishes for texture and a mild nutty flavour. Cassava flour is available in most supermarkets and Afro-Caribbean food shops.

content.text: This recipe serves 8 and takes about 2 hours 30 minutes from start to table, plus overnight soaking if you use dried beans. Feijoada is a dish that fills the house with a deep, smoky smell and gets better the longer it sits, which makes it suited to a weekend afternoon when you have time to let it do its thing.

If you are using dried beans, soak them in cold water overnight and drain before cooking. Tinned beans work well and cut the time significantly. The key to a good feijoada is layering the pork: cook the bacon or pancetta first to render its fat, then brown the pork shoulder in that same fat before adding the beans. Smoked chorizo or linguica goes in later so it does not break down completely. Taste for salt at the end, as the smoked meats can be quite salty on their own.

items.prepNote: dried and soaked overnight, or 2 x 400g tins, drained

content.text: If using dried beans, drain the soaked beans and place in a large pot. Cover with cold water by 5cm and bring to the boil. Simmer for 1 hour until just tender, then drain and set aside. If using tinned beans, skip this step.

In a large heavy pot, heat 1 tbsp of the oil over medium-high heat. Add 200g smoked bacon or pancetta, cut into lardons, and cook for 5 minutes until the fat has rendered and the meat is golden. Remove and set aside.
Brown the pork shoulder chunks in the same pot in batches, adding the remaining oil if needed. Do not crowd the pan. Each batch should take 3 to 4 minutes to colour properly. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion to the pot and cook for 8 minutes until soft and starting to colour. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute.

Return the bacon and pork shoulder to the pot. Add the cooked or tinned beans and enough water to cover by about 3cm. Add 3 bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook for 1 hour, stirring occasionally.
Add 200g smoked chorizo or linguica, sliced into rounds, and cook uncovered for a further 30 minutes until the stew has thickened and the pork shoulder is very tender. Season carefully with salt.
Serve over plain white rice, scattered with fresh coriander and a squeeze of lime. Put orange slices on the side and pass the
at the table for people to sprinkle over as they like.

attrs.symptom: Beans are still hard after a long cook
attrs.cause: Salt added too early can prevent beans from softening, or the beans are very old
attrs.fix: Do not add salt until the beans are tender. Old dried beans can take significantly longer, so keep simmering and top up water as needed.

attrs.symptom: Stew is too thin and watery
attrs.cause: Too much liquid added, or not enough simmering time uncovered
attrs.fix: Remove the lid and simmer on medium heat for 20 to 30 minutes to reduce. You can also mash a ladleful of beans and stir them back in to thicken the broth.

attrs.cause: Smoked meats vary a lot in salt content and can make the broth very salty
attrs.fix: Add a peeled raw potato to the pot and simmer for 15 minutes to absorb some of the salt, then discard. A squeeze of lime juice also helps balance the saltiness.

content.text: Feijoada is eaten across Brazil but Saturday is its day. In Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo, restaurants fill up at lunchtime with families ordering the full spread: stew, rice, fried kale, orange slices and a cold beer. At home it is the kind of meal that takes all morning to cook and keeps people at the table all afternoon.
